subject: DIF with survey weigths via logistic regression, possible?

messages.author: 447e2f2c316a6cae
messages.subject: DIF with survey weigths via logistic regression, possible?
parts:
Hi!
some weeks ago I asked in crossvalidated whether there was an R package for examining DIF by means of logistic regression, that could deal with survey weights. Phil Chalmers answered that mirt package is suitable for this and suggested to have a look at the package documentation. Unluckily I have not found any reference to DIF analysis apart from IRT models, which are a good solution anyways but I need the logistic regression approach. 

What I've done so far is computing the models for a 3 factor graded response model via multipleGroup() function, and kept the configural invariance model. Once I enter the specifications into the DIF() function, there is no way to choose anything else than the parameters of the model (a and d as you all know). How to proceed now? Is anyways possible to do what I need, or was it a misunderstanding?

Best wishes, thanks for your help
Regina Velázquez

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: DIF with survey weigths via logistic regression, possible?
parts:
Hi Regina,

You'll notice that multipleGroup() has a ... argument, meaning that other arguments not found in this documentation can be passed. help(mirt) contains the other possible arguments that can be passed to this function, one of which is survey.weights. What you need to do is supply a vector of weights for each case, where the sum of this vector is equal to the number of rows in your data. E.g., if you wanted the first half of your responses to be worth three times as much as the second half of the responses then survey.weights <- c(rep(3/2, N/2), rep(1/2, 2/N)). Supplying this to multipleGroup() will weight the likelihood accordingly, and from there you can use Wald or likelihood-ratio comparisons for DIF. HTH.

Phil

P.S. You definitely don't want configural invariance for DIF testing. Choose a set of anchor items and free the latent variance/mean terms to equate the groups, then continue with DIF. Otherwise your tests will contain population drift effects, and therefore DIF testing will be inappropriate.
